newsitem.title: USA: Dollar surges as investors hunt for higher yields.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surges as investors hunt for higher yields.

text.p: The dollar rallied sharply against most major currencies Wednesday following the strength in U.S. treasury markets.
Dealers said demand for the U.S. currency was strong as investors bought U.S. treasury instruments to lock in interest rates that were high in comparison with those in other industrial nations.
The Italian lira also rallied as a result of similar demand, they said.
U.S. bonds rallied on investor relief after Federal Reserve policy makers declined to raise interest rates at a meeting Tuesday, dealers said.

The Italian lira surged against the Japanese yen and the German mark, helping the dollar rally against those currencies as well. Late in the session, the lira broke below 1,000 to the mark and posted a two-year low at 996.

"Italy's bond market had a great day and that euphoria snowballed into the lira," said Jay Wertheimer, senior foreign exchange trader at Banco di Sicilia in New York. "After that we saw a wave a mark selling."
The dollar late Wednesday rose to 1.5167 marks from 1.5015 at Tuesday's close and to 110.49 yen from 109.07.
The British pound fell to $1.5610 from $1.5655. The dollar also rose to 1.2410 Swiss francs from 1.2250, but stood little changed at Canadian $1.3666 from C$1.3669.
Dealers also cited optimism that Italy might meet the strict financial requirements to qualify for a proposed single European currency for bolstering the lira.
"There's a feeling that Italy might get its act together in time to qualify," said Wertheimer.

Meanwhile, an International Monetary Fund report Wednesday hinted that Germany may need to continue lowering domestic interest rates, even as U.S. interest rates seem certain to rise in coming months.
Higher interest rates tend to bolster the dollar by increasing the returns on dollar-denominated assets.

"Interest rate differentials were a major reason for the day's action. It was a little selling of yen for lira early and it turned into marks for lira," said Greg Perman, chief dealer at Credit Commerciale de France.
The dollar began its rally overnight in Tokyo as investors abandoned the yen, dealers said.
By the start of New York trading, the dollar had reclaimed nearly all of the ground it lost Tuesday and it extended the rally as the session continued.
"The yen selling move started pretty much from the get-go in Tokyo. There was good interest to sell yen for dollars," said Thomas Arnold, chief dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank.

Mutual fund investors initially sold the dollar Tuesday afternoon on disappointment over the Fed's decision to leave interest rates steady, but as the U.S. currency recovered, many investors nervously bought it back.
"A lot of fund managers sold the dollar at poor levels Tuesday. Today they were re-establishing their positions," Arnold said.
Having benefited from broad buying interest on Wednesday, the dollar now appears poised for continued gains and should test 1.52 marks and 111 yen in the near future, dealers said.
"The buying in Japan really turned things around. The dollar has appreciated nicely," Wertheimer said.
